title: Social Comparison
description: We evaluate our own worth, abilities, and emotions by comparing ourselves to others. This can motivate us upward (comparing to those better) or make us feel better downward (comparing to those worse).
shortDescription: We evaluate our own worth, abilities, and emotions by comparing ourselves to others. This can motivate us upward (comparing to those better) or make us feel better downward (comparing to those worse).

sections.title: What It Is
sections.content: We evaluate our own worth, abilities, and emotions by comparing ourselves to others. This can motivate us upward (comparing to those better) or make us feel better downward (comparing to those worse).

sections.title: How It Actually Appears
content: Scrolling Instagram makes you feel inadequate because everyone’s life looks perfect.
A colleague gets promoted, and you suddenly feel your own career is stagnant—even though nothing changed for you.
After a bad day, you watch a reality show about people with chaotic lives and feel a little better about your own.

sections.title: Common Behaviors
content: Frequently checking others’ achievements, salaries, or lifestyles.
Mood swings based on how you rank compared to friends or coworkers.
Using others as a benchmark for “where I should be by now.”

sections.title: Real Phrases
content: “Look at her—she has it all together.”
“At least I’m not doing as badly as him.”
“Why can’t I have what they have?”

sections.title: Warning Signs
content: Your happiness depends on outperforming others.
You feel inferior after social media use.
You avoid people who are doing better than you, or you seek out those doing worse.

sections.title: Why It Works
sections.content: Leon Festinger (1954) proposed that humans have an innate drive to evaluate themselves, and when objective measures aren’t available, they use other people. Upward comparison can inspire or discourage; downward comparison can boost self‑esteem but reduce empathy.

sections.title: Protection Strategy
content: Compare yourself to your past self, not to others. Track your own progress.
Limit exposure to highly curated social media.
When you notice comparison making you feel bad, ask: “Is this person’s situation actually relevant to my life?”

sections.title: Common Mistakes
content: Thinking you should eliminate all comparison. Some is natural and motivating. The goal is to control it, not be controlled by it.
Assuming downward comparison is harmless. It can make you complacent or cruel.

sections.title: Real Scenario
sections.content: A graphic designer earns a good salary and enjoys her job. Then she discovers a colleague earns 10% more. Suddenly, she’s miserable and feels undervalued. Her job hasn’t changed, her bills haven’t changed, but her comparison point shifted, and it ruined her satisfaction.

sections.title: Key Insight
sections.content: Other people’s lives are not a mirror. When you measure yourself by someone else’s ruler, you’ll always come up short in your own eyes.
